messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Vinh's Reckoning

Vinh Nguyen is a forty-year-old investigative journalist whose career has been defined by a willingness to pursue stories others would not. Seven years ago, while reporting on human trafficking networks in Southeast Asia, he was detained by security forces in a facility he was never officially supposed to have entered. For three days, he was interrogated and tortured—beaten, deprived of water, subjected to electrical shocks applied to his torso and limbs. His captors demanded he reveal his sources. He did not. What remains of those seventy-two hours exists in his mind as fragments: the smell of the room, the voice of one interrogator whose name he can still hear in his nightmares, the sensation of his own body failing him, moments of consciousness giving way to darkness he cannot now retrieve. He cannot reconstruct the sequence of events with any coherence. When he tries to deliberately recall the details—a practice his therapist once suggested—the memory resists him, sliding away or presenting itself in disconnected flashes that feel less like lived experience and more like scenes from a film about someone else. The extremity of what happened has taken on an almost unreal quality, as though his mind refuses to fully integrate the experience as his own.

After his release and return to the United States, Vinh attempted to resume his career. For the first two years, he managed. He filed stories, attended editorial meetings, maintained the professional demeanor that had always come naturally to him. But gradually, the texture of daily life began to feel contaminated. When he heard children crying—at a restaurant, in a grocery store, on the street—his body would flood with a panic he could not explain or control, and within minutes his mind would splinter, fragments of the detention surfacing unbidden. The sound of a child's distress had become fused with something in the interrogation, though he could not say what. Dizziness would follow, a sensation of the ground tilting beneath him that forced him to grip whatever was nearest. Hearing names similar to his captors'—even in casual conversation, even on television—would trigger the same cascade: startle, disorientation, a creeping sense that the past was collapsing into the present. Each trigger seemed to open a door to the memory fragments, but not in a way that allowed him to process or resolve them; instead, the fragments came without sequence or meaning, leaving him more disoriented than before.

These triggers accumulated consequences that Vinh came to manage through avoidance. When he felt the dizziness beginning, when he anticipated the panic that might follow exposure to certain sounds or names, he began to withdraw from his social world. He stopped attending the informal drinks his colleagues organized after work, claiming exhaustion or deadlines. He declined dinner invitations from friends he had known before the detention, finding that being in their presence—people who knew him as he had been—activated a conviction he had come to harbor: that they could see something in him now that marked him as damaged, that his captors had left visible traces on his person that others could detect. This belief that he was exposed, fundamentally defective in a way that was apparent to anyone who looked closely enough, made socializing feel unbearable. He had come to believe that something essential in him had been broken or corrupted, that he had been forced to act in ways that violated everything he understood about his own character, and that this violation was written across his face and body like a scar. Rather than risk the shame of being perceived this way, he simply withdrew.

His eating became another arena of control. In the facility, food had been withheld as punishment. Now, seven years later, Vinh found that restricting his intake—sometimes skipping meals entirely, sometimes eating only small amounts he could carefully monitor—gave him a sense of agency his body had been denied during the torture. When he felt threatened, when the triggers activated his hypervigilance and he found himself watching the people around him for signs of imminent harm, undereating became a way to manage the anxiety, as though reducing his physical presence might reduce his visibility and risk. The less he ate, the lighter he felt, the easier it seemed to disappear. This restriction also served another function: it occupied his mind with rules and calculations, pushing aside the rumination that otherwise consumed him. He would dwell obsessively on how the detention might have been prevented—different choices in his reporting, different security measures, different decisions about where he went and when. Controlling his food intake was a way of controlling something, of preventing further loss, even as the prevention rumination itself had become a trap, a loop of self-blame that never resolved.

The avoidance and undereating, however, created their own feedback. As Vinh isolated himself and his physical health declined, the world around him began to feel increasingly dangerous. His hypervigilance intensified. He would jump at ordinary sounds—a car door closing, a telephone ringing, the unexpected voice of a colleague in the hallway—reactions that seemed absurdly disproportionate but which he could not suppress. He had developed a habit of watching people closely, searching their faces and body language for any indication that they might harm him, as though the threat that had been realized once could materialize again at any moment. This constant scanning for danger meant he was never truly at ease, and the fatigue of that vigilance fed back into his conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with him, that his nervous system had been permanently altered by what had happened, that he was no longer the person he had been. When the negative appraisals intensified—the sense that he was exposed, defective, that he had been violated in ways that made him unfit for normal human connection—they seemed to trigger new cycles of threat perception and avoidance. He would avoid situations more aggressively, restrict his eating further, ruminate more intensely on what he should have done differently.

Vinh's work as a journalist has suffered considerably. He has taken a leave of absence twice in the past three years. His editor has noticed his absence from the office, his reluctance to take on field assignments, the way he seems diminished when he does appear. His divorce, finalized two years ago, was in part a consequence of his withdrawal and the shame he carried about his perceived defectiveness—his ex-wife had wanted to help, but he could not bear to be seen, could not tolerate her proximity when he was certain she could perceive the damage in him. He lives alone now, in an apartment he rarely leaves except for necessary errands. He has lost significant weight. His sleep is fragmented, interrupted by nightmares he cannot quite remember upon waking but which leave him in a state of dread. What finally brought him to seek help was a panic attack at the newspaper's offices two weeks ago, triggered by a child crying in the lobby—a visiting family member of someone in the building. Vinh had frozen, then fled to the bathroom, where he remained for over an hour. His hands had shaken for the rest of the day. He realized, sitting alone in his apartment that evening, that the life he had constructed around avoidance was no longer sustainable, that something had to change, though he remains deeply afraid that acknowledging the full reality of what happened will destroy him entirely.
